facts.raw_span: 1 day of chest pressure
subjective fevers, rhinorrhea, a dry cough, and sinus congestion
3 hours of substernal pressure that resolved spontaneously
constant chest pressure radiating to the right jaw, diaphoresis, and 1 episode of vomiting
Vital signs obtained in the Emergency Department were within normal limits
Cardiac examination revealed a regular rate and rhythm, normal point of maximum impulse without lifts, and no murmurs, rubs, or gallops in supine, sitting, or standing positions
Initial serum troponin I level: 6.18 ng/mL
Elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein
ECG Findings: Normal sinus rhythm, ST-segment elevations with PR-segment depression in leads II, III, and aVF, ST-segment depression in lead V1, and PR-segment elevation in lead aVR
Coronary angiography: Normal coronary arteries
left ventricular end-diastolic pressure 12 mm Hg
Transthoracic echocardiogram: Normal results

concepts.why: The patient presented with chest pressure, elevated troponin levels, and ECG changes, which are consistent with acute coronary syndrome.
The patient had elevated inflammatory markers and ECG changes, which could be indicative of myocarditis.
The patient presented with chest pain and ECG changes, which are consistent with pericarditis.
The patient had symptoms of cough and sinus congestion, which could be indicative of a pulmonary embolism.
The patient presented with vomiting and chest pain, which could be indicative of gastroesophageal reflux disease.
The patient presented with chest pain and jaw pain, which could be indicative of costochondritis.
The patient had symptoms of fever and cough, which could be indicative of a viral pericarditis.
The patient presented with cough and sinus congestion, which could be indicative of acute bronchitis.
It explains the normal coronary arteries found in the coronary angiography, which rules out coronary artery disease as the cause of the chest pressure.

rationales.F04: Chest pressure radiating to the jaw is a common symptom of acute coronary syndrome and pericarditis.
rationales.F07: Elevated troponin levels are a strong indicator of myocardial infarction and myocarditis.
rationales.F09: ECG findings of ST-segment elevations and PR-segment depression are consistent with pericarditis and myocarditis.
rationales.F10: Normal coronary arteries on angiography rule out acute coronary syndrome.
